title: Silencing Jason Arday’s accuser only makes him a martyr
gist: Alan Rusbridger argues that Nathan Cofnas, the 'race realist' academic who accused the late Cambridge professor Jason Arday of plagiarism, should be allowed to speak at Oxford's Oriel College but met with scorn and rebuttal rather than cancellation, since silencing him feeds his martyr narrative. He uses Oxford and Oriel admissions and staffing data to rebut Cofnas's claim that DEI is undermining higher education.

insights.claim: Cancelling Nathan Cofnas's Oxford event would reinforce the martyr image he is cultivating, whereas letting him speak and challenging him robustly is more likely to lead to him being forgotten.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Free-speech controversies amplify fringe figures when institutions attempt to silence them.
insights.quote: Making him a martyr will have the opposite effect.
insights.locator: But it is right that he

insights.claim: Since Jason Arday's resignation and death, Cofnas has gained a platform on podcasts and YouTube, turning from an obscure figure into a self-styled martyr.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Controversy-driven attention economics reward provocateurs with audience growth.
insights.quote: And, yet, the podcast invitations keep coming.

insights.claim: Cofnas reposted an image depicting himself as a Christ-like martyr on the cross, which the author calls a crucifixion with all the glory and none of the cost.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Illustrates deliberate grievance branding by online commentators.
insights.quote: The result is a crucifixion with all the glory and none of the cost.

insights.claim: Universities should ensure controversial speakers are both tolerated and properly challenged, and audiences owe them no respect; Cambridge's 2020 proposal that academics must treat each other with 'respect' was rightly rejected.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Frames the institutional free-speech approach universities are likely to be pressed to adopt.
insights.quote: There’s no cause for Oxford students to listen to Cofnas with respect.
insights.locator: Cambridge University got into deep water

themes.theme: Data rebutting the DEI claim at Oxford

insights.claim: Of Oxford University's roughly 2,000-strong academic workforce, only about 14 academics identify as black, or 0.7 per cent.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Hard data undercuts claims that DEI hiring has transformed elite university staffing.
insights.quote: there appear to be just 14 academics identifying as black—or 0.7 per cent
insights.locator: As far as the University of Oxford

insights.claim: Of Oriel College's 198 undergraduate intake last year, only two were black, consistent with a three-year average of 2.3 black students a year.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Elite admissions diversity remains very low despite DEI rhetoric.
insights.locator: Last year, out of an intake

insights.claim: Oriel's intake included 98 state-school students against 93 from independent schools, even though only 7 per cent of UK pupils attend private schools.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Private-school overrepresentation at Oxford persists, relevant to UK education policy debates.
insights.quote: Just 98 students came from state schools against a healthy 93 from independent schools
insights.locator: Last year, out of an intake

insights.claim: Oxford missed its 2009 target for increasing students from disadvantaged backgrounds in six of the following eight years.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Widening-participation targets at elite universities have repeatedly underdelivered.
insights.locator: Of course, there has been hand-wringing

insights.claim: Oxford's later pledge to recruit a further 23 low-income students amounts to less than one per college and fewer than the Wykehamists who typically arrive each year.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Access targets remain marginal relative to elite-school pipelines.
insights.locator: The university then set another target

insights.claim: The Cecil Rhodes statue at Oriel remains in place six years after the Governing Body voted to remove it.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Institutional decisions on contested heritage often stall in implementation.
insights.quote: Rhodes did not, in the end, fall.
insights.locator: Oriel College should feel like safe ground

insights.claim: Cofnas's Cambridge collegiate association was severed in 2024 after he promoted 'race realism', though a 2025 Cambridge inquiry found his views did not breach the law or free-speech regulations.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Shows the legal and regulatory limits on universities acting against offensive speech.

insights.claim: Cofnas argues that without DEI initiatives there would be virtually no black professors at elite universities, a view fellow sociologists denounced as shoddy and harmful.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Context on the contested claims driving the campus speech fight.

insights.claim: After Arday's death, Ghent University briefly suspended Cofnas and then allowed him to resume research but not teaching, while Trump's State Department threatened to review funding.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: US government intervention in foreign academic speech disputes adds a geopolitical dimension to campus controversies.
insights.quote: Trump’s State Department threatened to review funding.
insights.locator: Plenty of Cofnas’s colleagues at Ghent

insights.claim: A 2020 letter by nine professors to Philosophical Psychology accused Cofnas of presenting 'racial realism' misleadingly as science and of falsely claiming race-IQ research is suppressed.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Academic consensus is against Cofnas's claims.

insights.claim: Multiple investigations failed to substantiate Cofnas's plagiarism allegations against Jason Arday, whose suicide in August followed a media witch hunt.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Highlights the human and reputational costs of online pile-ons over unproven allegations.
